answer:
## Headline answer (as the pre-specified criterion directed)

**The relation between SES and chances of degree completion is not, on this evidence, affected by racial lines.** In the headline total-effect model (adjusted for ability, sex, family size only), the SES-by-race interaction fails the pre-specified likelihood-ratio test: **LRT chi2(2) = 1.333, p = 0.513**; Wald chi2(2) = 1.374, p = 0.503; dAIC = **−2.67** (the interaction model is *worse* by AIC). Corroborated by a parametric bootstrap (p = 0.514, B = 800) and a Firth-penalised Wald test (p = 0.478). The companion percentile-adjusted estimand agrees: LRT chi2(2) = 1.745, p = 0.418, dAIC = −2.26.

So, per your second condition: **race appears chiefly as a difference in level rather than a difference in slope.** SES raises the odds of a degree (OR **1.231**, 95% CI 1.045–1.450, p = 0.0127 per +1 SD); the race terms remain jointly associated with completion (LRT 2 df, chi2 = 6.10, p = 0.047), but the slopes do not differ.

## Race-specific SES slopes (odds ratio per +1 SD SES, robust HC1 CIs)

| estimand | White (ref) | Black | Hispanic |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Total effect (headline)** | 1.189 (0.990–1.428), p=.065 | 1.502 (1.040–2.168), p=.030 | 1.191 (0.754–1.881), p=.455 |
| Partially direct (companion) | 1.191 (0.991–1.431) | 1.563 (1.079–2.262) | 1.204 (0.767–1.890) |

Interaction terms themselves: Black×SES = +0.234 (p = 0.246); **Hispanic×SES = +0.002 (p = 0.995), imprecisely estimated on 19 events**.

## Marginal probabilities (total-effect model), covariates standardised within race

| race | SES −1 SD | mean | +1 SD | pp change | ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| White | 2.75% | 3.32% | 3.99% | +1.24 | 1.45× |
| Black | 1.08% | 1.31% | 1.58% | +0.50 | 1.46× |
| Hispanic | 1.21% | 1.46% | 1.75% | +0.54 | 1.45× |

The *proportional* gradient is near-identical in all three groups, while the absolute gap persists: even a high-SES Black or Hispanic respondent (≈1.6–1.8%) sits below a low-SES White respondent (2.75%). This is exactly the level-not-slope pattern.

## The one inconvenient result, reported rather than promoted

The **crude** interaction *is* significant (LRT chi2(2) = 9.574, p = 0.0083; dAIC +5.57; crude slopes White 1.17, Hispanic 1.65, Black 2.07). I do **not** advance this as effect modification. The diagnostic explains why it vanishes: within-race correlations of SES with ability/family size differ by group (corr(SES,ability): Black 0.355, Hispanic 0.435, White 0.399; corr(SES,family size): Black −0.026, Hispanic −0.066, White +0.250), so within-stratum crude slopes shift on adjustment (Black 0.726→0.411, Hispanic 0.499→−0.025, White 0.161→0.230). The apparent crude modification is largely compositional.

## Robustness and power

Categorical SES×race (6 df) p = 0.961; SES²×race p = 0.730; re-levelling to Black as reference reproduces LRT = 1.333/p = 0.513 exactly; fully race-specific model, extra slope differences p = 0.195; pooled-minority sensitivity p = 0.366; SES×sex exploratory p = 0.949; Firth converged (max |penalised score| ≈ 1e-8). **Power (condition 3):** a Black−White slope difference must exceed 0.454 log-odds/SD (OR ratio ≈ 1.58) and a Hispanic−White difference 0.598 (OR ratio ≈ 1.82) for 80% power. The Hispanic term is therefore suggestive-of-nothing, not evidence of equality; dropping the 7 Hispanic/top-SES-quartile degree holders swings its slope from +0.17 to −0.42, which shows how fragile it is.

## Conditions honoured

(1) The two estimands are never merged — reported side by side, headline = total effect. (2) The LRT governed and the null is stated plainly, with the descriptive rate differences explicitly *not* promoted. (3) Hispanic treated as fragile: joint 2-df test primary, level kept separate, imprecision named, no claim of equality. (4) Percentile direction kept as a stated assumption; sign behaves sensibly once fitted (β = +0.605, OR 1.83, p = 2e-07) and **the variable was never re-signed**.

## Limitations

No curriculum variable exists in the file despite the study description promising one, so programme rigour cannot be controlled (class percentile proxies it imperfectly). The data are a complete-case subset (8,773 records, no missing values) with **no weights, strata or PSUs**, so SEs assume simple random sampling and are likely understated; generalisation is limited to respondents with valid class rank and observed degree status, and no survey-style precision is claimed. Ability and family-size adjustments are contestable, and the reversal of the race coefficients under adjustment (unadjusted Black OR 0.42 → adjusted 1.86) is a warning against causal reading: all statements are associational.

Deliverables: executed scripts 01–04 with logs, coefficient/OR tables, slope tables, marginal-probability tables, Firth and bootstrap outputs, and the written hypothesis in analysis/HYPOTHESIS.md.

payload.hypothesis: Among NLS respondents, socioeconomic status is positively associated with the chance of completing a BA degree, but this socioeconomic gradient is not modified by the race of the individual once ability, sex and family size are held constant. Each additional standard deviation of SES raises the odds of degree completion by about 1.23 (95% CI 1.05-1.45, p = 0.013), and the SES slope is statistically indistinguishable across Hispanic, Black and White respondents (LRT for the SES-by-race interaction chi2(2) = 1.33, p = 0.513; Wald p = 0.503; AIC worsens by 2.67; parametric-bootstrap p = 0.514; Firth-penalised Wald p = 0.478; race-specific odds ratios per SD of SES: White 1.19, 95% CI 0.99-1.43; Black 1.50, 1.04-2.17; Hispanic 1.19, 0.75-1.88). Race instead acts chiefly as a difference in level rather than a difference in slope: Black and Hispanic respondents complete degrees far less often than White respondents (1.32% and 1.44% vs 3.54%), and race keeps an independent association with completion after adjustment (joint LRT chi2(2) = 6.10, p = 0.047) whose direction reverses once ability, sex and family size are held constant (Black OR 1.86, 1.20-2.89; Hispanic OR 1.34, 0.81-2.23). A proportional gradient therefore coexists with a persistent absolute gap: moving from one SD below to one SD above mean SES raises the modelled probability of a degree by 1.45-fold in every group, yet a high-SES Black or Hispanic respondent (about 1.6-1.8%) remains below a low-SES White respondent (2.75%). An SES-by-race interaction is visible in the unadjusted data (crude LRT p = 0.008) but it does not survive adjustment and is largely compositional, since SES tracks ability and family size differently within the minority groups than within the White group; it is reported descriptively and not claimed as effect modification. The Hispanic-by-SES term is imprecisely estimated on 19 degrees among 1,323 respondents and is underpowered (differences below about 0.60 log-odds per SD are undetectable at 80% power), so it is characterised as uninformative rather than as evidence of equality. The same conclusion holds in the companion percentile-adjusted (partially direct) estimand (interaction p = 0.418), so the finding does not depend on the mediator adjustment. These are associations under an assumed simple-random-sampling design in a complete-case subset of the cohort with no weights, strata or curriculum measure, and no causal claim is made.
payload.workflow: 1) Inspection of data/nls_ses_processed.csv (8,773 records x 8 variables, unique CASE ID, no missing values or sentinel codes, no curriculum variable present). 2) Logistic regression of BA DEGREE COMPLETED on standardised SES with a three-level race factor (White reference) and heteroskedasticity-robust HC1 standard errors, on all 8,773 complete cases (236 events). 3) Two estimands kept strictly separate: TOTAL effect (ability, sex, family size) as headline and PARTIALLY DIRECT effect (additionally adjusting for PERCENTILE IN CLASS, a plausible mediator), each as a nested pair of main-effects vs SES-by-race interaction models. 4) Pre-specified primary criterion: likelihood-ratio test of the 2 interaction terms, cross-checked with a joint Wald test, delta-AIC, race-specific slopes with confidence intervals (linear combinations), and g-computed marginal probabilities at SES = -1/0/+1 SD standardised within each racial group. 5) Robustness: Firth penalised likelihood (with the penalised LR reported but not chi2-calibrated), a B=800 parametric bootstrap of the interaction LRT under the main-effects null, categorical-quartile and quadratic SES specifications, re-levelling with Black as reference, a fully race-specific model, stratified fits, a pooled-minority sensitivity, a one-cell influence check and an explicit minimum-detectable-effect calculation. 6) All steps executed in analysis/01..04 python scripts with logged output and CSV result tables; written hypothesis in analysis/HYPOTHESIS.md.
